metaDescription: Six De'Longhi space heaters compared across oil-filled radiators, a ceramic tower, a convection panel and a capsule, with the real trade-offs of each design.
expertTake: The De'Longhi Dragon Digital is the best fit for most bedrooms because its oil-filled body is silent and the 24 hour timer makes overnight use sensible. The Capsule is the value pick for a desk or small office. Anyone who wants fast heat on demand should skip the oil radiators and look at the ceramic tower instead.
introParagraphs: One brand can cover a whole range of heating methods, and that is the case here. A single maker sells sealed oil-filled radiators, fan-driven ceramic towers, silent convection panels and compact fan heaters, and each one behaves differently in a room even though all of them top out at the same electrical ceiling.

So the useful question is not which model is the strongest but which delivery method suits the space. Slow, silent radiators reward patience, fans reward speed, and panels reward careful placement. Matching the method to your routine matters more than the badge on the front.

products.name: De'Longhi Dragon Digital Oil Radiator 1500W
products.description:
The Dragon Digital is an oil-filled radiator, which means the 1500W element heats sealed oil, and the oil warms the metal fins that radiate into the room. That indirect path is why the unit is silent and keeps radiating after the element cycles off, though it also means it takes longer to warm a room than a fan heater does.

The maker credits an unusual fin layout with 75 percent more radiant surface area than its older RadiaS design, and a bigger radiating area means the surface can run cooler for the same heat. The digital panel and 24 hour timer are the reasons to choose this over the mechanical Dragon: you can program warm-up before you wake instead of leaving it on all night.

Oil radiators are heavy and sealed, so there is little to maintain, but they do demand stable footing. Roll it on its casters across hard floors only, keep the cord clear of the wheels and never drape laundry over the fins, which is a real fire risk with any radiator. If it ever leaks oil, retire it; the sealed body is not a repairable part.
products.bestFor: Bedrooms and living rooms where silence and programmable timing matter.
cons: Slow to warm a cold room

products.name: De'Longhi Dragon Oil Radiator 1500W, Child Lock
products.description:
This is the Dragon without the digital display: a selector for temperature and power, a programmable 24 hour timer and a child lock, on the same sealed oil radiator body. Think of it as the more affordable sibling to the Dragon Digital, trading the LED panel for plainer controls.

Because there is no fan, noise is essentially absent, which is the strongest argument for the Dragon family in a bedroom. Warm air moves by convection, rising off the fins and drawing cooler air in underneath, so the room heats evenly but slowly. The child lock is a practical extra in a house where small hands reach for knobs.

Placement matters more than with a fan heater, because a radiator needs open space around it for convection. Keep it at least a few feet from curtains and furniture, plug it directly into a wall outlet and let it cool fully before moving it. The oil is sealed for the life of the unit, so there are no filters or reservoirs to look after.
products.bestFor: Quiet rooms where a simple selector beats a menu.

products.name: De'Longhi Oil-Filled Radiator 1500W, ComfortTemp
products.description:
The standard De'Longhi radiator centres on ComfortTemp, a feature that automatically maintains a chosen temperature by adjusting power. The idea is to keep the room steady rather than swinging between hot and cool, which an oil radiator is well suited to because its mass smooths out the swings.

Its thermal slot design, according to the listing, pushes heat into the room while keeping the surface temperature low. That is a real consideration with radiators, whose fins can get hot enough to be uncomfortable to touch. It lacks the Dragon models' timer, so you will switch it off yourself.

Expect the usual oil-radiator routine: a slow start, a long coast after power cuts and a heavier body than a fan unit. Clear a space around the fins, keep it away from damp floors and bathrooms, and move it by the handle only when it is cool. For a steady, quiet background heater, it is a straightforward choice.
products.bestFor: Steady background warmth in a bedroom or study.

products.name: De'Longhi Ceramic Tower 1500W with Remote and Timer
products.description:
If you want warmth fast, the ceramic tower is the pick in this lineup. It blows air across a hot ceramic element and swings it across the room with a motorised oscillation, so it warms the space far sooner than any of the oil radiators.

The listing credits a quiet technology that cuts noise by half, which is worth taking as a relative claim, since fan heaters are louder than radiators in any case. An ECO Plus function adjusts heat and power on its own to avoid wasted running, while the remote and timer make bedside use realistic. Against the oil-filled models, you gain speed and lose silence.

Because a tower is tall and narrow, give it a flat hard floor and keep it away from doorways. Vacuum the grille at the start of heating season so dust does not bake on the element, and unplug it when it is not needed. It makes sense if you warm a room for an hour and then switch off.
products.bestFor: People who want quick warmth with a remote and timer.
pros: Warms a room faster than radiators
cons: Fan noise despite the quiet claim

products.name: De'Longhi Convection Panel Heater 1500W
products.description:
A convection panel heats air as it flows past a flat element, with no fan and no oil. That makes this De'Longhi quiet like a radiator but lighter and thinner, and its ability to mount on a wall frees the floor.

The ECO Plus function automatically adjusts heat and power, so it behaves like a thermostat that trims energy use. The listing positions it for medium to large rooms, but 1500W is 1500W, so treat the claim as optimistic in a drafty space. Against the Dragon radiators, you give up the heat-storage coast, since a panel cools quickly once the element stops.

A panel is easier to move than a radiator but should still stay clear of curtains. If you mount it on a wall, use hardware suited to the wall type and keep the cord tidy. It suits a hallway, a nursery-adjacent room or any place where floor space is scarce.
products.bestFor: Quiet, space-saving heat in a bedroom or office.
pros: No fan so it is quiet
cons: Cools quickly when it cycles off

products.name: De'Longhi Capsule 1500W Compact Heater
products.description:
The Capsule is the small one: a stylised, lightweight body that stands on a desk or a floor and delivers 1500W of fan-forced warmth. It also offers a fan-only function, so it can move air in summer.

It is built for small spaces and personal warmth, so think of it as a way to heat only the room you are in, not the whole house, which is how the listing frames the saving. Compared with the ceramic tower, it is simpler and smaller, with no remote and no oscillation listed. It heats quickly because it is a fan unit, with the noise that implies.

Use it on a hard flat surface, keep it away from paper and cables and dust the grille before each heating season. A compact heater is easy to forget, so unplug it at the wall when you leave the room.
products.bestFor: Desks, small offices and spot warming.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Dragon models are oil-filled and silent, while the ceramic tower and Capsule are fan-driven. A radiator takes longer to warm a cold room but keeps radiating after the element cycles off. A fan unit is faster and louder. Decide whether you value silence or speed before looking at any model number. A useful middle path is to run the ceramic tower for twenty minutes to take the chill off and then switch to a Dragon for the long evening, but that only makes sense if you own both, so most buyers should simply pick the method that matches how they use the room.

The Dragon Digital and Dragon both carry a 24 hour timer, and the ceramic tower adds a remote and timer. A heater you can schedule is a heater you do not forget on. The standard radiator and the Capsule have neither, so you turn them off yourself.

A larger radiating surface can run cooler for the same heat. The maker says the Dragon has 75 percent more radiant area than the RadiaS design, while the standard radiator cites a thermal slot to keep the surface cooler. That matters in a home with children or pets.

ECO Plus and ComfortTemp both adjust output to avoid overshooting. They do not change the conversion of electricity to heat, which is close to total in any electric heater, but they cut the time at full power. The ceramic tower and panel include ECO Plus; the standard radiator uses ComfortTemp.

The convection panel can mount on a wall, which frees floor space, while the radiators need open ground and casters. The Capsule sits on a desk. Measure before buying. A radiator needs open space on all sides to set up its convection loop, so a unit wedged beside a sofa will heat the sofa and little else. The panel is the better answer for a narrow hallway or a room where furniture claims every wall, while the Capsule suits a desk where nothing else needs the space.
Three oil radiators and the panel have no fan. The tower and Capsule do. If you sleep lightly, choose the radiators or the panel even though they warm more slowly.

specDecoder.watchFor: The three radiators here are slow to warm a cold room.

specDecoder.watchFor: The De'Longhi panel can be wall-mounted.

specDecoder.watchFor: The tower and Capsule use this method.

specDecoder.meaning: A programmable timer schedules on and off periods across a day. It prevents all-night running and lets you pre-warm a room.
specDecoder.watchFor: The two Dragon models list it; the standard radiator does not.

specDecoder.watchFor: Savings claims depend on room and use, so treat percentages as best case.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heating method
howWeEvaluated.description: We sorted the six De'Longhi models by how they deliver heat: oil radiator, ceramic fan, convection panel and compact fan. Method decides noise and warm-up speed more than any spec. The lineup covers each one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls and timing
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared timers, remotes and automatic modes. The Dragon Digital offers a 24 hour timer and LED display, while the standard radiator relies on ComfortTemp. Programmability scored higher for bedrooms.

howWeEvaluated.title: Surface and safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at radiating surface, child lock and thermal design claims. The Dragon family emphasises a large radiant surface and a child lock. A cooler surface is a real benefit in a busy home.

howWeEvaluated.title: Space and mounting
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how each unit fits a room, from the wall-mountable panel to the desk-sized Capsule. Floor space is often the limiting factor. Weight and casters also counted. A sealed radiator is heavy enough that moving it daily becomes a chore, so we favoured lighter bodies for people who relocate a heater between rooms and heavier ones for a permanent spot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We read recurring themes on warm-up speed, noise and control feel from owner feedback. These supported the ranking without driving it. The set runs from silent oil radiators to a quick ceramic tower.

cards.label: Radiators
cards.text: The Dragon Digital, Dragon and standard radiator are silent and keep radiating after cycling off. They suit bedrooms and steady use but warm slowly.

cards.label: Fan heaters
cards.text: The ceramic tower and Capsule warm a space quickly. They suit short sessions but add noise.

howToChoose.note: Choose a Dragon for bedrooms; choose the tower or Capsule for fast, short bursts.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for silence, a timer, a low-temperature surface and a child lock. A radiator body suits sleep because there is no fan hum.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Dragon Digital offers silence, an LED display and a 24 hour timer, and the Dragon with Child Lock adds the lock.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more on the Dragon Digital if you want programmable overnight heat, or the ceramic tower if you want remote control.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save with the Capsule or standard radiator if you only need basic warmth without timers.

maintenance.why: Dust blocks airflow and smells when heated. Use a dry cloth on radiators and a brush on fan units.
A radiator is heavy and can tip on a damaged caster. Tighten the base before moving it.
A warm plug signals a poor connection. Retire the heater if its plug shows discolouration.
Never drape laundry on the fins and keep three feet from curtains. Radiators stay hot after power cuts.
Keep radiators upright in a dry space. Laying one on its side can disturb the oil.

faq.a: The three Dragon-style oil radiators and the convection panel have no fan, so they are effectively silent. The ceramic tower and Capsule use fans.

faq.q: Are the oil-filled models cheaper to run?
faq.a: Not in total energy, since electric heaters convert nearly all power to heat. They can feel cheaper because they cycle and coast, but the cost per hour at 1500W is the same.

faq.q: Which is best for a baby's room?
faq.a: A fanless radiator with a child lock, such as the Dragon, suits quiet rooms. Keep any heater well clear of cribs and follow the maker's distance guidance. Remember that a radiator stays hot to the touch for a while after it is switched off, so a child lock stops the controls being changed but does not make the metal cool. Place it behind a barrier or in a corner out of crawling reach if the room is used by a toddler.

faq.q: How long do oil radiators last?
faq.a: The oil is sealed for the life of the unit, so the main wear points are the thermostat and casters. Leaking oil is a sign to retire the heater.

faq.q: Can I mount the panel on a wall?
faq.a: Yes, the convection panel can be freestanding or wall mounted, with hardware suited to the wall.

It cuts time at full power, but the saving depends on the room and your habits. Treat percentage claims as best case. The honest way to cut a bill with any of these is to heat one occupied room and close its door, because a 1500W heater cannot warm a house, and the lower the thermostat setting the fewer minutes the element spends drawing full current.
